perpetuate

/per-PEH-choo-ate/ — stress on second syllable · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To perpetuate something is to cause it to continue or persist, often for a long time.

Statues and street names perpetuate the memory of the city's founders.

Example

By teaching these old recipes to her grandchildren, Carmen perpetuated her family's culinary traditions for another generation.

Perpetuate is more precise than 'continued' because it emphasizes the deliberate cause to continue. Carmen is actively passing on traditions, making them persist into the future—that's perpetuating, not just letting something happen on its own.

Your Turn

Answer correctly to continue.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

continue: Continue means to keep an activity or process going without stopping - the meeting continued, the rain continued. It is neutral and moment-to-moment. Perpetuate reaches further: to perpetuate something is to deliberately push it onward into the future, often across years or generations.

preserve: Preserve means to protect something - a building, a recording, a stretch of forest - so it survives unchanged and undamaged. Preserving guards a thing from harm. Perpetuating keeps a practice or belief alive: you preserve an old letter, but you perpetuate the tradition of writing them.

sustain: Sustain means to keep something going by feeding it the support it needs - meals sustain a hiker, donations sustain a shelter. It is about supplying support right now. Perpetuate is about reach through time: making something persist long after the present moment.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

discontinue: to stop something and not resume it

terminate: to bring something to a final end

Where it sits · how long it is kept going — discontinue → pause → immortalize → perpetuate

discontinue vs. perpetuate: Discontinue is the direct opposite of perpetuate: discontinuing ends a practice for good, while perpetuating keeps it going year after year.

pause vs. perpetuate: Pause sits on the weak, opposite side of perpetuate — pausing interrupts something briefly, while perpetuating pushes it onward with no end in sight.

immortalize vs. perpetuate: Immortalize outdoes even perpetuate: to perpetuate a memory is to keep it alive for a long time, but to immortalize it is to seal it in a form meant to last forever.

Which word fits?

Answer correctly to continue.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — per-

Prefix — per-: through, thoroughly (Latin)

Root — petu

Root — petu: to seek, go toward (from Latin petere, as it appears in perpetuus, 'continuous')

Suffix — -ate

Suffix — -ate: verb-forming, to make or cause (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Per- ('through') + petu ('to seek, go toward,' from Latin petere, as it appears in perpetuus, 'continuous') + -ate ('to make or cause'): something perpetuated keeps going through — made to continue onward without interruption, often for a very long time.

Use the root in a new word: perpetual

Use the root in a new word: perpetual: A perpetual calendar hangs in the clockmaker's shop window, its brass dial engraved back in 1898 — per- ('through') plus pet- ('go').

Word Building

Word Choice

formal / literary

Perpetuate is the word for deliberately making something continue, especially across time or generations. Use it when someone or something actively keeps a tradition, memory, practice, or belief alive. For simple continuation, 'continue' is more neutral and direct.
